clue.text: Airmen, well into journey, scratched message

indicators.note: these words go into the journey word, splitting it around them

parts.note: a go is a trip or turn, so journey gives GO
the RAF, Royal Air Force, is a body of airmen
well as in healthy means fit

explanation.surface: Some pilots, deep into a long trip, scrawled a note somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The singular of graffiti is a single inscription scratched or drawn on a wall.

clue.text: Stupid and senseless to incarcerate son

indicators.note: to incarcerate is to lock up, so the senseless word holds the son inside it

parts.note: senseless means inane, empty of sense

explanation.surface: A judgement on locking up one's own boy: dim and pointless.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, a stupid idea is called crazy or mad, an everyday loose synonym.

clue.text: Taverners' spy turned up in secret society

indicators.note: the overturned spy word sits in the secret word

parts.note: inner can mean private or secret, as in inner thoughts

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word for spy is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to spy is to peek

explanation.surface: Pub landlords' informant is uncovered within a hidden brotherhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taverners'' looks like the cricket charity, but here it simply means innkeepers.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverners are those who run taverns, i.e. pub landlords; the possessive in the clue matches the plural form here.

clue.text: See 10
See 11
Passing mention

parts.note: a passing mention seems a brief remark in conversation, but here passing is death, and the mention is a notice of it

explanation.surface: A brief aside in conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's death notice mentions someone who has passed away, so it is literally a mention of a passing.

clue.text: Swimmer ordered Cobra beer to be taken round

indicators.note: the beer word is to be taken round the shuffled letters, enclosing them

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: ordered here means put in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone in an Indian restaurant orders a Cobra beer to be brought over.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobra is a brand of Indian beer often served in British curry houses, which makes 'ordered' look like a restaurant order rather than the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuna species, a fish, so a swimmer in the crossword sense of a sea creature.

clue.text: Husband rejected nosegay, grasping small aromatic plant

indicators.note: the overturned word grasps the small letter, holding it inside
rejected means sent back, so the nosegay word is turned round

parts.note: a nosegay is a small bunch of flowers, a posy

explanation.surface: A husband spurns a bunch of flowers but grabs one little fragrant herb instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns POSY into YSOP; 'grasping' puts S inside to give YSSOP after H.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragrant herb of the mint family, used in medicine and cooking, hence an aromatic plant.

clue.text: Plants sister next to copper in labyrinthine lair

indicators.note: the sister and copper pieces sit in the scrambled lair letters
labyrinthine means mazy and tangled, so the letters of lair are jumbled

parts.note: a nun is called Sister
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A nun and a policeman find themselves in a monster's maze-like den.
explanation.walkthrough: 'labyrinthine' turns LAIR into RALI, split around NUNCU.
explanation.definitionFit: Buttercups belong to the genus whose Latin name this is, given in its plural form for plants.

clue.text: Stout schoolboy can joke where Ungraded replaces A

parts.note: a billy or billycan is a tin can for cooking over a campfire

indicators.note: the ungraded letter takes the place of the letter A in the joke word

parts.note: banter is joking talk
U is the British film classification for universal, suitable for all, i.e. unrestricted or ungraded

explanation.surface: A fat pupil can tell a joke in which an unmarked grade stands in for an A.
explanation.walkthrough: BANTER with U for A gives the surname. 'Ungraded' is the U film certificate.
explanation.definitionFit: The famously fat, greedy pupil of Greyfriars School in Frank Richards's stories, beloved of British children's comics.

clue.text: 10 4 creator's plain ridiculous when crossing road

parts.note: frank means plain-speaking, candid
rich in the sense of that's rich means laughably absurd

indicators.note: the when word crosses the road, sitting astride it

parts.note: as can mean when, as in as I left

explanation.surface: Someone says the stout schoolboy's author is clearly absurd for walking across a street.
explanation.walkthrough: 's is 'is' acting as a link. The name is the pen name of Charles Hamilton.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name under which Charles Hamilton wrote the stories of the fat Greyfriars pupil, hence his creator.

clue.text: Islanders in volunteer force wallop Scotsmen

parts.note: the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force
to wallop is to hit
Ian is a typical Scottish name, so Scotsmen are Ians

explanation.surface: Members of a volunteer army thump some Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of a South Pacific island in French Polynesia, so islanders.

clue.text: Eric drunkenly presses buzzer for cold booze

indicators.note: the shuffled name presses round the buzzer, squeezing it inside
drunkenly suggests reeling, so the letters of Eric are scrambled

parts.note: a bee buzzes, so a buzzer

explanation.surface: Tipsy Eric leans on the doorbell, wanting a chilled drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunkenly' turns ERIC into ICER, which surrounds BEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lager brewed partly frozen, served very cold and fairly strong, so a chilled alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Borders in resurgence and Greek publisher in form again

indicators.note: borders are edges, so the edge letters of resurgence are taken

parts.note: OUP is Oxford University Press, a publisher

explanation.surface: A political revival in the Scottish Borders, with a Greek publisher reshaping things.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring or come together again into a group or formation, e.g. troops after a setback.

clue.text: 10 4's institution for older brothers?

parts.note: grey hair goes with age, so grey suggests older
friars are addressed as Brother

explanation.surface: A question whether the fat schoolboy's school is meant for senior siblings.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional boarding school attended by the fat pupil in Frank Richards's tales.

clue.text: See 21
PM gone to shake out hay on moorland

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: to ted is to spread out mown hay for drying
a heath is open uncultivated moorland

explanation.surface: A farmer leaves to turn hay on the moors.
explanation.definitionFit: Conservative Prime Minister of the UK 1970-74, who died in 2005, so a late premier.

clue.text: Energy expended, departs soul venue

indicators.note: expended means used up, so the energy letter is spent and removed

parts.note: dies as in departs this life
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Exhausted, a performer leaves the soul music club.
explanation.definitionFit: The classical underworld where souls of the dead go, also its ruler's name, hence a place for souls.

clue.text: Politicians brought in to intimidate columnist once

indicators.note: the politicians are brought into the intimidate word

parts.note: to deter is to put off by fear
MPs are Members of Parliament

explanation.surface: MPs are called in to scare a former journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel, the late Daily Mail gossip writer, was a famous newspaper diarist in the past.

clue.text: Still time to ride competitively

parts.note: even can mean still, as in even better

explanation.surface: There is still time to enter a horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventing is the equestrian sport of dressage, cross-country and jumping, so a verb for riding in competition.

clue.text: Regularly target a certain prize

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of target a is taken

parts.note: sure means certain

explanation.surface: Aim consistently at a guaranteed award.
explanation.definitionFit: To prize something is to value it highly, cherish it; both work as verbs, and as nouns too.

clue.text: Finances in order, presumably

parts.note: money kept neat would literally be a neat total, but the phrase means a large amount

explanation.surface: Someone's accounts look well kept.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a sizeable amount of money, read literally as an orderly total.

clue.text: Rotten omelette for he who rails against 10 4

indicators.note: a rotten omelette is spoilt, so these letters are broken up

parts.note: one who rails against something is against it, versus, abbreviated V

explanation.surface: A bad egg dish for someone who complains about the fat schoolboy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 16 letters of OMELETTE FOR HE WHO plus V are rearranged. The Remove was Bunter's form at Greyfriars.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname given to the fat Greyfriars pupil, for his round spectacles, after his school form.

clue.text: Character witness on ecstasy cutting loose

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading

indicators.note: the ecstasy letter cuts into the loose word

parts.note: free means loose, unrestrained
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A witness speaks for someone's character while high and on the loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who vouches for an applicant's character in a reference is a character witness of sorts.

clue.text: Salad ingredient little girl spots outside

indicators.note: the spots word goes outside the little girl's name

parts.note: a rash is an outbreak of spots
Di is short for Diana, a girl's name

explanation.surface: A child notices something round a bowl of salad.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisp peppery root vegetable often sliced into salads.

clue.text: See 21
Worried guard finally joins train

indicators.note: the guard's last letter joins onto the train word

parts.note: to exercise is to train

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of guard

explanation.surface: A railway guard's last stop links up with a train.
explanation.definitionFit: Exercised can mean anxious or agitated, as in exercised about a problem.

clue.text: Stephen, a crusader, holds up defeat

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the held letters are read upwards
the phrase Stephen, a crusader holds the letters within it

explanation.surface: A crusader called Stephen staves off a loss.
explanation.walkthrough: In stephEN A Crusader the letters ENAC read upwards give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, to cane an opponent is to beat them soundly.

clue.text: Poetic content from Tees is nonsense!

parts.note: Tees is the setter, so from his point of view Tees is becomes I am
BS is slang for nonsense

explanation.surface: The setter confesses that he talks rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Tees is the setter of this puzzle, so 'Tees is' read from his mouth is I AM.
explanation.definitionFit: Metrical feet of an unstressed then stressed syllable, the stuff verse lines are built from.

clue.text: Ring supremo with security group's backing

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the security group is reversed

parts.note: NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a security alliance; the 's is 'has' or 'is'

explanation.surface: A crime ring boss has the support of a security firm.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief of the gods in Wagner's Ring cycle, the German name for Odin.

clue.text: Estuary bear skinned one struggling

indicators.note: skinned means the outer letters of bear are removed

parts.note: a striver is one who struggles

explanation.surface: A bear with its fur off flails about near a river mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The New York tidal strait is technically a saltwater estuary, not a river.
